objective: Connect to and consume Azure services
stem: At what level is Azure OpenAI model quota ultimately constrained?

options.text: The Azure subscription
The Microsoft Entra tenant
The individual model deployment
The resource group holding the resource

explanation: Microsoft is explicit that quota is not enforced at the tenant level — the highest level of restriction is the Azure subscription. Deployments then draw from that allocation, which is why two deployments in the same subscription compete for the same pool.

whyWrong.B: A tenant can hold many subscriptions, each with its own quota.
whyWrong.C: A deployment consumes quota; it is not where the ceiling is set.
whyWrong.D: Resource groups are a management boundary and carry no quota.

objective: Connect to and consume Azure services
stem: In what unit is Azure OpenAI quota allocated to a deployment, and how does the request rate relate to it?

options.text: Tokens per minute, with requests per minute derived from it
Requests per minute, with tokens derived from request size
Concurrent connections, with tokens counted for billing
Provisioned throughput units, for every deployment type

explanation: TPM is the allocation, and RPM follows from it at a ratio published per model and version. That is why a workload of many tiny requests can hit the request ceiling while its token usage still looks comfortable.

whyWrong.B: The relationship runs the other way — tokens are the allocated unit.
whyWrong.C: Azure OpenAI does not allocate quota by connection count.
whyWrong.D: PTU applies to provisioned deployments, not to Standard ones.

hint: One of the two numbers is allocated and the other is calculated from it. Ask which one you actually request more of.

objective: Connect to and consume Azure services
stem: A latency-critical production workload must have predictable response times at sustained high volume, not best-effort throughput. Which deployment type fits?

options.text: Provisioned throughput, which reserves dedicated capacity
Global Standard, which routes to whichever data centre has availability
Data Zone Standard, which routes within one data zone
Global Batch, which processes requests asynchronously

explanation: Standard deployment types give consistent latency only while you stay inside your usage tier; above it, latency becomes variable. Provisioned throughput reserves capacity, which is what turns latency into something you can promise rather than hope for.

whyWrong.B: Global Standard optimises for availability across regions, so latency varies with where a request lands.
whyWrong.C: Data Zone Standard narrows the routing geographically but is still shared, best-effort capacity.
whyWrong.D: Batch is for work that can wait; it is the opposite of latency-critical.

hint: Three of these share capacity with other customers. Ask which one stops sharing.

objective: Connect to and consume Azure services
stem: Data residency requires that inference for EU customers never leaves the EU, but the team still wants Azure to route across data centres for availability. Which deployment type meets both?

options.text: Data Zone Standard, which routes within a Microsoft-defined data zone
Global Standard, which routes to the best-available data centre worldwide
Standard, pinned to one region with no routing at all
Global Batch, which is processed wherever capacity exists

explanation: Data Zone Standard is the middle option that exists precisely for this: dynamic routing for availability, but bounded by a data zone such as the EU. Global Standard gives up the boundary; a single-region Standard deployment gives up the routing.

whyWrong.B: Global routing is exactly what the residency requirement forbids.
whyWrong.C: This satisfies residency but abandons the routing the team asked for.
whyWrong.D: Batch has the same global routing problem, and is asynchronous besides.

hint: Two requirements pull in opposite directions. Look for the option that is deliberately in between.

objective: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
stem: An ingestion job batches chunks into a single `/embeddings` call to reduce overhead. What are the two hard ceilings it must respect per request?

options.text: 2,048 inputs in the array, and 300,000 tokens summed across all inputs
1,000 inputs in the array, and 128,000 tokens summed across all inputs
No input limit, but 8,192 tokens per individual input
16 inputs in the array, matching the default max_tokens

explanation: Both limits bite in practice: an array is capped at 2,048 inputs, and the sum of tokens across the whole request at 300,000. A batching loop that only counts inputs will still fail once the chunks get long.

whyWrong.B: Neither figure is right, though they look plausible against other model limits.
whyWrong.C: There is a per-request array limit, and the token cap is on the request total.
whyWrong.D: 16 is the old GPT-4 vision default for `max_tokens`, which is unrelated.

hint: Two ceilings, not one. A batch can be legal by one measure and illegal by the other.

objective: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
stem: A RAG service returns 429s during traffic spikes. Which two responses does Microsoft recommend before asking for more quota? Choose two.

options.text: Implement retry logic with backoff in the client
Ramp the workload up gradually rather than in sharp steps
Open a new Azure OpenAI resource in the same region to double the allocation
Cache the API key in memory to reduce round trips
Lower the deployment's TPM so requests are spread out

explanation: Retry with backoff and a gradual ramp are the two the guidance leads with — most 429s during a spike are transient, and sudden load changes are what provoke them. Moving quota between deployments, or requesting more, comes after.

whyWrong.C: Quota is constrained at subscription level, so another resource does not conjure new allocation.
whyWrong.D: Caching the key reduces Key Vault calls, not calls to the model.
whyWrong.E: Reducing TPM lowers the ceiling you are already hitting.

hint: Two options treat the spike as transient and survivable. The rest try to buy or reconfigure your way out.

objective: Secure, monitor, and troubleshoot Azure solutions
stem: Monitoring shows token usage sitting comfortably below the deployment's quota, yet clients still receive 429 responses. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The request-rate ceiling is hit before the token ceiling
The metric is wrong and should be recalculated from the billing export
Quota has been silently reduced because the subscription is idle
The deployment has been moved to a different region

explanation: Quota has two dimensions. A workload of many small requests exhausts the derived requests-per-minute allowance long before it approaches the token allowance, which is why a token-usage chart can look healthy while callers are being throttled. Microsoft documents this as a specific cause of 429s below quota.

whyWrong.B: The metric is measuring what it says; it is simply not the dimension being exceeded.
whyWrong.C: Quota is not reduced for inactivity, and tier changes only move allocations upward.

hint: You are watching one of the two numbers. Ask what the other one is doing.
